accepted_examples.german: Der Star der Show war Tom.
accepted_examples.english: The star of the show was Tom.
accepted_examples.note: Show is used as an event/performance; the English translation is the same sense.

accepted_examples.german: Was für eine Überraschung, Sie hier zu sehen!
accepted_examples.english: What a surprise to see you here!
accepted_examples.note: Überraschung means surprise here; the sentence and translation are natural.

accepted_examples.german: Stehst du mit deinen Eltern in Kontakt?
accepted_examples.english: Are you in contact with your parents?
accepted_examples.note: In Kontakt stehen is the idiomatic phrase for being in contact; the translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Der Krieg gegen Drogen ist ein politischer Krieg.
accepted_examples.english: The war on drugs is a political war.
accepted_examples.note: Drogen means drugs in the political phrase Krieg gegen Drogen; the translation is accurate.

accepted_examples.german: Die Regierung ging hart gegen die Minderheit vor.
accepted_examples.english: The government clamped down on the minority group.
accepted_examples.note: Regierung means government; the idiomatic English clamped down on renders ging hart gegen ... vor.

accepted_examples.german: Tom saß unter einem Baum und trank Wein.
accepted_examples.english: Tom was sitting under a tree, drinking wine.
accepted_examples.note: Wein means wine and is used in an ordinary drinking context.

accepted_examples.german: Er ist entfernt mit ihr verwandt.
accepted_examples.english: He is distantly related to her.
accepted_examples.note: Entfernt means distantly in the expression entfernt verwandt; this matches the entry sense distant.

accepted_examples.german: Ihr Haus steht genau gegenüber der Bushaltestelle.
accepted_examples.english: Her house is just opposite the bus stop.
accepted_examples.note: Gegenüber is correctly used as a preposition meaning opposite, with a dative noun phrase.

accepted_examples.german: Das Baby hat sich in den Schlaf geweint.
accepted_examples.english: The baby cried itself to sleep.
accepted_examples.note: Schlaf means sleep in the result phrase in den Schlaf weinen; the translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Die Erde ist vom All aus betrachtet wunderschön.
accepted_examples.english: Seen from space, the earth is very beautiful.
accepted_examples.note: Wunderschön means very beautiful; the translation is accurate.

accepted_examples.german: Kommt schon, Leute! Das ist nicht mehr witzig.
accepted_examples.english: Come on, guys. This isn't funny anymore.
accepted_examples.note: Witzig means funny in this context; the sentence is modern and clear.

accepted_examples.german: Haben Sie mit dem Kopf genickt?
accepted_examples.note: Genickt is the correct past participle of nicken; the translation says nod your head.

accepted_examples.german: Er hatte einen guten Blick auf die Papiere.
accepted_examples.english: He had a good look at the papers.
accepted_examples.note: Blick is used in the sense look/view; the English matches.

accepted_examples.german: Es ist zu schwer, um es zu bewegen.
accepted_examples.note: Bewegen is the infinitive after zu and means move; the sentence is direct.

accepted_examples.german: Es ist schwer zu erkennen, ob Tom sein Haar färbt oder nicht.
accepted_examples.english: It's hard to tell whether Tom dyes his hair or not.
accepted_examples.note: Haar is used as head hair; the example is grammatical and matches a common sense of the noun.

accepted_examples.german: Ich bin noch nicht bereit zu antworten.
accepted_examples.english: I'm still not ready to give an answer.
accepted_examples.note: Antworten is correctly used as the infinitive after bereit zu and means answer/respond.

accepted_examples.german: Der Präsident saß auf dem Stuhl, mit dem Rücken zum Fenster.
accepted_examples.english: The president was sitting in the chair with his back to the window.
accepted_examples.note: Präsident means president in the German sentence; chair is translated as the piece of furniture Stuhl.

accepted_examples.german: Ich wünschte, wir könnten mehr Zeit miteinander verbringen.
accepted_examples.english: I wish we could spend more time together.
accepted_examples.note: Miteinander means together/with one another; the translation is accurate.

accepted_examples.german: Er ist weder für noch gegen den Plan.
accepted_examples.english: He is neither for nor against the plan.
accepted_examples.note: Weder is correctly paired with noch and means neither in this sentence.

held_examples.german: Das ist ein Geheimnis, daß du hüten mußt.
held_examples.reason: The source uses obsolete spellings daß and mußt. Replace them with current dass and musst while retaining the same clear example.

held_examples.german: Tom gab zu, Maria ermordet zu haben.
held_examples.reason: The source uses ermordet as a verb participle, while the entry is the adjective murdered. Use an attributive adjective example.

held_examples.german: Ich fuhr rechts ran, und stieg aus.
held_examples.reason: The source has an incorrect comma between two coordinated predicates with the same subject. Keep the example and correct the punctuation.

held_examples.german: Das habe ich schon immer an dir geliebt.
held_examples.reason: The source uses geliebt as a verb participle, although this entry is an adjective. Use an attributive adjective example.

held_examples.german: Ich wusste nicht, dass du zu Besuch kämest.
held_examples.reason: The source uses the rare literary subjunctive kämest; replace it with a natural contemporary sentence that demonstrates the noun.

plural_reviews.usage_note: Use Akte for act/deed; Akten belongs to administrative file usage.

plural_reviews.usage_note: Plural is unchanged: Spezies.

plural_reviews.note: Duden lists Eigentume but marks the plural rare.

plural_reviews.note: Betriebe is correct for countable operations/business units; in Betrieb means a device is operating and is usually singular.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Plural Betriebe; the technical state in Betrieb is normally singular.

plural_reviews.note: Neffe is a weak masculine noun and forms Neffen.

plural_reviews.note: For pieces of furniture, Möbel is the unchanged plural; the colloquial sense of an awkward object has no plural.

plural_reviews.usage_note: Reise only for rice varieties; ordinary rice is usually singular.
